683-Federal Budget Deficit and Debt 
684-Even before the pandemic, the Federal Government’s deficit and debt were trending higher.  At 
685-the end of FY 2020, the Federal Government posted a deficit of $3.13 trillion (15.0 percent of 
686-GDP), up $2.15 trillion from the $984 billion deficit (4.6 percent of GDP) posted in FY 2019.  
687-The primary deficit (which excludes net interest payments) was 13.3 percent of GDP in FY 
688-2020, up from 2.9 percent in FY 2019.  Federal receipts totaled $3.42 trillion in FY 2020, down 
689-$44 billion (1.3 percent) from FY 2019.  Net outlays for FY 2020 were $6.55 trillion, up $2.1 
690-trillion (47.3 percent) from FY 2019.  As of April 2021, the federal deficit was $225.6 billion, 
691-bringing the 12-month total deficit to $3.58 trillion. 
692-     The Treasury’s borrowing limit is suspended until July 31, 2021.  At the end of FY 2020, 
693:gross federal debt was $26,945.4 billion.  Federal debt held by the public, or federal debt less the 
694-debt held in government accounts, rose from $16.80 trillion at the end of FY 2019 (79.2 percent 
695-of GDP) to $21.0 trillion by the end of FY 2020, or 100.3 percent of GDP.  As of April 2021, 
696:gross federal debt was $28,174.7 billion, while federal debt held by the public totaled 
697-$22,056.1 billion. 
698-Economic Policy 
699-The U.S. government has responded to the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic with a range of 
700-significantly countercyclical fiscal and monetary policies, including an unprecedented level of 
701-fiscal assistance and a reduction in the key policy interest rate to near-zero. 
702-On the fiscal side, Congress authorized a record-setting economic aid package of roughly $2.7 
703-trillion in March 2020, and a second, smaller package was passed in December 2020.  The aid 
704-included two rounds of direct Economic Impact Payments to low- and middle-income Americans, 
705-a temporary weekly federal addition to normal state unemployment compensation, and broadened 
706-eligibility for unemployment benefits to the self-employed and gig workers.  Tax payments were 
707-postponed in 2020, loan payments were delayed for borrowers of federally backed student loans, 
708-and a moratorium on evictions was instated.  This slew of policies boosted disposable incomes and 
709-has help American households to weather the pandemic. 
710-In addition, Treasury and the Small Business Administration (SBA) launched the Paycheck 
711-Protection Program (PPP) less than a week after its authorization at the end of March 2020.  The 
712-federal government worked directly with private lenders and used their infrastructure to hasten 
713-how quickly businesses could receive funds.  In less than two weeks, the PPP had exhausted its 
714-initial funding: it had processed nearly 1.7 million loans worth $342 billion.  After a second 
715-appropriation, the PPP provided 5.2 million loans by the time of the program stopped accepting 
716-applications in August, worth over $525 billion. 
717-In 2021, President Biden signed the American Rescue Plan (ARP) into law.  The ARP provides 
718-an additional $1.9 trillion in economic aid, primarily through Economic Impact Payments and 
719-direct aid to low- to middle-income families and to the economically vulnerable.  It also assists 
720-state and local governments, provides additional funding for addressing COVID-19 infections 
721-

723-and vaccinating the population, creates new loans and grants for small businesses, and provides 
724-another $274 billion in PPP funds.   
725-On the monetary policy side, the Federal Reserve’s Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) 
726-resumed monetary easing in early March 2020.  The previous cycle of easing had begun in July 
727-2019 but was paused very early in 2020, owing to buoyant economic conditions at that time.   
728-At the January 2020 meeting, the Federal funds rate target was unchanged at a range of 1½ to 2 
729-percent, and in the accompanying statement, the Committee observed that at the time, “the 
730-current stance of monetary policy is appropriate to support sustained expansion of economic 
731-activity, strong labor market conditions, and inflation near the [Fed’s 2 percent target].”   
732-However, the pandemic led to an inter-meeting move.  On March 3, the FOMC announced a 50-
733-basis point cut in the target range to 1 to 1¼ percent, and on March 15, at another unscheduled 
734-meeting, the FOMC cut the target range by 100 basis points to 0 to ¼ percent.  (The scheduled, 
735-March 17-18 FOMC meeting was cancelled.)  
736-At its scheduled meetings from April 2020 through April 2021, the FOMC left the target range 
737-for the federal funds rate unchanged.  In each of the accompanying statements for those 
738-meetings, the Committee noted that it expects to maintain this FFR target range “until it is 
739-confident that the economy has weathered recent events and is on track to achieve its maximum 
740-employment and price stability goals.” 
741-The Federal Reserve has also implemented large-scale purchases of Treasury securities and 
742-agency mortgage-backed securities.  Importantly, the Federal Reserve assuaged market worries 
743-by using its Section 13(3) authority to establish numerous emergency lending facilities and   
744-leveraged capital provided by Treasury.  The existence of these facilities may have unlocked 
745-financial markets and mitigated the risk of the public health crisis from becoming a financial 
746-crisis, but they were only authorized on an emergency basis through December 31, 2020.  
747-Treasury extended capital for some of these lending facilities through March 31, 2021, and these 
748-have now expired.
